articles.title: Watch: Floods rock Japan's Nagoya as streets turn into sea, manhole explodes
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Nagoya, a city in Japan in began assessing the damage from record rainfall on Wednesday after Japan’s highest-level flood warning for the Shonai River.
articles.body: Nagoya, a city in Japan in began assessing the damage from record rainfall on Wednesday after Japan’s highest-level flood warning for the Shonai River was lowered overnight and evacuation instructions were withdrawn. Nagoya City said the Disaster Relief Act had been applied across the city from September 8, opening the way for emergency assistance in areas affected by the flooding.The first official damage assessment released by the Aichi Prefectural Government on Wednesday reported three minor injuries — one in Nagoya and two in Kitanagoya. One house was partially damaged, while 16 homes were flooded above floor level and 27 below it. About 200 vehicles in Nagoya were also reported flooded and unable to move.The immediate river threat eased during the early hours of Wednesday. The Level 5 flood warning for the Shonai River was lowered to a Level 2 advisory at 12.40am, according to Jiji Press. Nagoya City separately said it withdrew a Level 4 evacuation instruction for the Yada River at 2.45am after conditions fell below the relevant threshold.Nagoya is the capital of Aichi prefecture in central Japan and home to about 2.35 million people, according to city data. The city is a major transport and industrial centre in the Tokai region.Record rain hits NagoyaThe emergency followed an exceptional spell of rain on Tuesday.Japan Meteorological Agency data show Nagoya received 104.5mm of rain in one hour on September 8, the highest hourly total recorded at the station since observations began in 1890. The previous record was 97mm, set in September 2000. Nagoya received 219.5mm of rain over the day, according to JMA.A video posted by the X account GlobeUpdate purports to show flooding in Nagoya during Tuesday’s downpour. The post cites the 104.5mm hourly rainfall figure, which matches JMA data.Heavy rain repeatedly hit Aichi and neighbouring Gifu prefecture as developed rain clouds passed over the same areas. Roads were inundated and transport was disrupted across Nagoya.Nagoya City said bus and subway services were affected and temporary refuge facilities were opened for people unable to return home after public transport was disrupted.The Associated Press reported that about 3,500 people sought shelter during the flooding.Highest flood warning issuedAs conditions deteriorated on Tuesday evening, Japanese meteorological and river authorities issued a Level 5 flood warning for the Shonai River.The Japan Meteorological Agency said the warning was issued on September 8 after the river reached conditions indicating an extremely high likelihood that a disaster had already occurred in designated flood-risk areas.Level 5 is the highest category in Japan’s five-tier disaster warning system. It is used when people may already be facing life-threatening conditions and immediate action to secure safety is required.Nagoya separately issued Level 5 emergency safety instructions in affected areas as the rain intensified.The warnings were gradually lowered as river levels receded overnight, shifting the focus by Wednesday morning from immediate evacuation to damage assessment and relief.Flooding hits Asian Games host cityThe flooding also came at a sensitive time for Nagoya, which is preparing to co-host the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games from September 19. About 400 athletes and staff who had already arrived for the Games were temporarily moved to higher ground during the heavy rain. They later returned after the evacuation order was withdrawn.More than 11,000 athletes from 45 countries and regions are expected to take part in the Games.Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa said the Games venues had suffered no major damage, according to AP, although some facilities reported roof leaks. Organisers expect the event to proceed as scheduled.With the highest flood alert lifted, authorities on Wednesday were turning to the scale of damage left by the September 8 downpour, even as relief measures under the Disaster Relief Act began to take effect.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: West Bank sanction row: Israel bars 12 British MPs from entering country
articles.summary: UK News: Israel prohibited 12 British MPs from entering the country, citing anti-Israel actions after the UK imposed sanctions on goods from Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar condemned the UK government and called for a response to what he termed hostile actions.
articles.body: Israel has barred 12 British MPs and a campaign group director from entering the country, with Foreign Minister Gideon Saar accusing them of anti-Israel and antisemitic activity.The move came after the UK government imposed restrictions on goods produced in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, escalating tensions between the two governments.Saar announced the measures on Tuesday, saying Israel was responding to what he described as hostile actions by the Labour government. He also criticised remarks made by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband in Parliament, calling his address "outrageous lies".The British officials and campaign figures affected are Jeremy Corbyn, Zarah Sultana, Naz Shah, Diane Abbott, Hannah Spencer, Carla Denyer, Sian Berry, Ellie Chowns, John McDonnell, Richard Burgon, Adrian Ramsay and Fahad Ansari, director of Riverway to the Sea.Saar said those targeted were "involved in antisemitic and anti-Israel activity, as well as those who deny the very existence of the State of Israel".The restrictions extend beyond the MPs. Israel will close the British Consulate in Jerusalem and remove British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre in Kiryat Gat, Saar said.Israel will also end British involvement in training Palestinian Authority security forces in the West Bank through the British Support Team in Ramallah.The measures follow increasingly sharp criticism of Israel from the UK government. Miliband accused Israel of "turning a blind eye" to the alleged ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank, where Palestinian communities have faced pressure from Israeli settlers.Saar said the Labour government had adopted a hostile position towards Israel since coming to power in 2024 and warned other governments against attempting to pressure Israel over its security and national interests."We did not return to our land after 2,000 years only to lose it under pressure from jihadists, Islamists, antisemites, far-leftists and wokes," Saar said.The Green Party, whose MPs are among those barred, rejected the Israeli government's decision and said it would continue campaigning on Palestinian rights."We will not be bullied into silence by the Israeli government," a party spokesperson said, adding that the ban strengthened its call for an arms embargo and broader sanctions against Israel.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Family of murdered teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
articles.summary: The parents of Celeste Rivas Hernandez say execution "would be perfect" if D4vd is found guilty.
articles.body:
The family of 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez has lobbied for the death penalty if D4vd is found guilty murdering their daughter.

D4vd, who was born David Anthony Burke, is charged with killing the teenager, whose dismembered body was found in the trunk of a Tesla car registered to his address on 8 September 2025. Burke has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

The death penalty is under a temporary ban in California, where Burke is due to stand trial, but in a statement Hernandez' family said execution "would be perfect" if the singer was convicted of murder.

In a related development, Hernandez's parents filed a civil lawsuit against Burke on Friday, seeking monetary damages including burial and funeral expenses.

The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple US media outlets , makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer.

Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter.

In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old.

Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times.

"At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday.

They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life".

In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard.

Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security.

Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times reported.

In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty.

In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution.

"If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney.

Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney . He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year.

Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".

"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.

His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit.

articles.title: A year after Charlie Kirk's murder, some comics are calling out jokes about his death
articles.summary: After initial grief following Charlie Kirk’s murder, less than a year later and the mainstream comedy world would resort to treating the event as material for a comedy roast.
articles.body: As the one-year mark since the murder of Charlie Kirk approaches this week, some comedians are calling out fellow comics for their jokes and reactions following the assassination of the conservative activist. In May, Pete Davidson made a joke about Kirk’s assassination during Netflix’s "The Roast of Kevin Hart" in Los Angeles. Yet even in today’s "anything goes" style in the world of entertainment, Davidson’s joke shocked some fellow humorists. Talking about fellow comedian Tony Hinchcliffe, Davidson said on May 10, 2026, "Tony reminds me of Charlie Kirk in that he’s definitely been on camera letting a guy unload in his throat." ROGAN TELLS ‘TRAITOR’ COMEDIANS CONDEMNING THE KEVIN HART ROAST TO ‘F--- ALL THE WAY OFF’ "I watched it, and the reaction, you know, was like a giant groan, which is not what you want as a comedian," performer and comedy writer Michael Loftus told Fox News Digital. "With Davidson, it’s like, ‘My reputation precedes me. I’m daring, I’m brash. I’ll say anything.’ Well, yeah, I’ll say anything about the guy who is not going to punch me back. You’re certainly brave about the guy who’s not in the room." Loftus, who met Kirk years ago at the nonpartisan political convention Politicon in Los Angeles, said that as a comedian, he’s "all about freedom of speech and the First Amendment," but described those who made jokes about Kirk as "just absolute cowards." Comedian Bryan Callen told Fox News Digital that satire has long helped keep rulers in check and prevented people from taking themselves too seriously. "You’re reminded that we’re all going to die someday," he said, explaining how comedy acts as a social equalizer and brings people together by highlighting human flaws. "But then there’s something called good taste and compassion and things that just don’t make you laugh because somebody was killed," he said. "When something terrible happens publicly, and you see somebody killed in front of their children and their wife, I think we need a button that says, ‘Wait, hold on…’" The joke generated backlash on social media. DISNEY UNDER FIRE AS ABC GRAPPLES WITH ANOTHER JIMMY KIMMEL CONTROVERSY Jimmy Kimmel ran into trouble days after the assassination as well. The "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" host was suspended by ABC after the comedian criticized the political reaction to Kirk’s assassination and erroneously implied the suspect in the case was a MAGA supporter. On Sept. 15, 2025, he said, "We hit some new lows over the weekend with the MAGA gang desperately trying to characterize this kid who murdered Charlie Kirk as anything other than one of them and doing everything they can to score political points from it." DISNEY ACCUSES TRUMP'S FCC OF ATTEMPTING TO 'SUPPRESS SPEECH' WITH LICENSE RENEWAL INVESTIGATION But ABC brought his show back less than a week after suspending it, following a controversy involving Disney, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, the Trump administration, ABC and its affiliates. The episode raised questions about whether government and political pressure exerted through broadcasters and regulators could influence what a comedian can say. Meanwhile, more than 400 entertainment figures, including Jennifer Aniston, Tom Hanks and Meryl Streep, signed an ACLU-backed open letter supporting Kimmel and warning against threats to free speech. Others, like comic book writer and horror novelist Gretchen Felker-Martin, who posted incendiary comments about Kirk right after his death, didn’t have such support. Felker-Martin had her "Red Hood" comic series canceled by DC Comics. The comic book publisher said posts or public comments that could be viewed as promoting hostility or violence were "inconsistent with DC's standards of conduct." For his part, comedian Trevor Noah turned his commentary about Kirk's death into a discussion of gun control rather than the debate over censorship and speech. Meanwhile, the sitcom "South Park" became part of the debate. The show had parodied Kirk just weeks before his death, and Kirk embraced the joke, calling it a "badge of honor." But after his murder, Comedy Central pulled the episode from its cable rotation. Loftus, who noted he’s been doing stand-up for years, said he often sees comedians, for example, have no problem making fun of Christianity when they’re actually joking about members of a religion known for turning the other cheek, which he said Kirk practiced. "I would love to see Pete Davidson’s material on Islam. He’s such a brave and incredibly thoughtful performer that surely he has some jokes about Islam," he said. "Oh, your Charlie Kirk stuff — yes, very edgy and brave of you. But surely there are some jokes about Muhammad." Fox News Digital reached out to Davidson for comment. Loftus argued that many in Hollywood who opposed Kirk's beliefs haven't gone back to Kirk's own material, which Loftus described as thoughtful and well-presented, with Kirk delivering his arguments with a smile and a warm heart. Callen described Kirk as a formidable intellect who could defend his positions and talk to people with whom he disagreed because he had studied their arguments more than his opponents had. Following Kirk, he said, never meant you had to be of one particular political persuasion. "What he would always say is, ‘If people stop talking and stop debating in good faith, very bad things happen.’ So, I think Charlie Kirk, in many ways, was reminding us that this — our country and its freedoms — took a long time to build, and so much of us now, it’s very easy to define what you’re against, and it’s actually very easy to build a following and clicks by taking a strong side and amplifying your monologue. But Kirk didn’t ignore nuance or having a discussion," Callen said. "Again, he had the respect to read the people he disagreed with and not just read, but try to understand from their perspective," he said. "He could tell you exactly what the Old and New Testament was, how it contributes to the very lives we live today. Not many people can do that. That takes a lot of effort," Callen added. "He earned his point of view. He earned it. It wasn’t based on attitude. It was based on research and thought, and immersing himself in the best that’s been taught and said." Loftus said that the message of common sense will ultimately succeed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The message that Charlie was sending out into the universe will certainly prevail. It’s just a matter of, you know, how long is it going to take and how much suffering will it take to get there?"

articles.title: In 2023, record storms nearly refilled Los Angeles reservoirs and shallow aquifers; deeper groundwater recovered only about 25% of what it had lost since 2006
articles.summary: US News: Los Angeles was drenched by historic storms, yet much of its lost groundwater stayed missing. Record-breaking rainfall in 2023 brought dramatic relief.
articles.body: Los Angeles was drenched by historic storms, yet much of its lost groundwater stayed missing. Record-breaking rainfall in 2023 brought dramatic relief to drought-stricken Southern California, nearly restoring water stored in Los Angeles-area reservoirs and shallow aquifers. But the recovery was far less complete underground. A study published in Science found that aquifers deeper than about 50 metres remained substantially depleted. Researchers estimated that only about 25% of the groundwater lost from these deeper aquifers since 2006 was restored after the exceptionally wet year.Extreme rain brought rapid reliefThe 2023 storms were remarkable in both intensity and duration. A series of intense atmospheric-river storms brought exceptionally heavy precipitation to California in early 2023, rapidly improving surface-water conditions after years of drought, according to Stanford researchers. The enormous volume of water rapidly improved surface conditions, filling reservoirs and allowing shallow groundwater systems to recover substantially. For a region that had experienced years of drought and extensive groundwater extraction, the turnaround appeared dramatic. But the researchers found that the apparent recovery at the surface did not extend equally into deeper underground water reserves.Deep aquifers remained depletedGroundwater does not respond to rainfall as quickly or uniformly as reservoirs and shallow aquifers. Water reaching the ground must move through layers of soil and rock before it can replenish deeper groundwater. The study found a clear difference with depth. Near-surface groundwater storage almost completely recovered following the wet 2023 season, while aquifers below roughly 50 metres remained substantially depleted. Only about one-quarter of the groundwater lost from these deeper systems since 2006 had been restored.The researchers tracked groundwater changes across the Greater Los Angeles region over roughly two decades. Their analysis showed that deeper aquifers had experienced a continuing depletion trend, in contrast to shallow groundwater, which fluctuated more closely with changes in weather and precipitation. That distinction is important because a wet year can create the impression that a drought has been completely reversed when substantial water losses remain hidden underground.Seismic waves reveal hidden waterOne of the unusual aspects of the research was how scientists measured changes in groundwater. Alongside conventional groundwater observations, the team used seismic ambient-field interferometry to track changes across the region, analysing seismic waves recorded by the region's earthquake-monitoring network. Seismic waves travel differently through underground materials depending partly on their physical properties. Changes in groundwater levels can therefore alter the way seismic waves move through the subsurface.By examining decades of seismic observations, researchers were able to develop what they described as seismic hydrographs, records that reveal changes in groundwater storage over time. This provided a way to examine groundwater recovery across different depths and over a much broader area than would be possible using individual wells alone.Why deeper water recovered slowlyThe contrasting response between shallow and deep aquifers reflects how difficult it is for stormwater to reach deeper underground layers. Heavy rainfall can quickly increase surface-water storage and replenish shallow groundwater. But reaching deeper aquifers requires water to move through substantial thicknesses of soil and rock. In an urbanised region such as Los Angeles, much of the rainfall can also become runoff rather than infiltrating deeply into the ground.As a result, a single exceptionally wet season cannot necessarily compensate for years of groundwater extraction. The researchers concluded that the enormous storms of 2023 were not enough to reverse the groundwater depletion that had accumulated during previous droughts. According to the lead study author and researcher Shujuan Mao, many more wet years would be needed for the deeper aquifers to fully recover.A warning beneath the wet yearThe findings highlight an important difference between surface-water recovery and groundwater recovery. Reservoir levels can rise rapidly after major storms, while underground reserves may take much longer to rebuild. This matters for the Greater Los Angeles region, where groundwater is an important water resource for millions of people. The study suggests that assessing drought recovery solely by looking at rainfall, reservoirs or shallow groundwater can give an incomplete picture of the region's water situation.The 2023 storms therefore delivered substantial relief, but they did not erase the legacy of prolonged drought and groundwater extraction. Beneath a landscape that appeared dramatically wetter, deeper aquifers continued to carry much of the deficit accumulated since 2006.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A school turned memorial: What remains of Iran's Minab site after deadly strike
articles.summary: Middle East News: Families often gather at the shattered remains of the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, southern Iran to grieve and remember the children who were ki.
articles.body: Families often gather at the shattered remains of the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, southern Iran to grieve and remember the children who were killed in a US airstrike on the school during the first day of the war.The school, once filled with classrooms, desks and children's drawings, now lies in ruins. Concrete hangs from exposed reinforcing bars, while classroom desks and chairs remain scattered inside and among the rubble. Colourful tree and flower decorations that once adorned the walls have survived amid the destruction.As volunteers search through the wreckage, they continue to recover remnants of the children's lives, including notebooks and a drawing stencil. Each item offers a small reminder of the children who were inside the school when it was hit.At a section of Minab's cemetery set aside for those killed at the school, families continue to mourn. Relatives return to clean the children's graves and pay their respects, keeping alive the memory of those lost in the strike.Some 120 children were killed when at least one missile hit the school on February 28, according to the account provided by the Associated Press, although a final accounting of those killed has not yet been made.Iranian state media have said 168 people were killed in that strike, most of them children.Why was the school hit?Trump initially blamed Iran after details of the strike emerged."In my opinion, based on what I've seen, that was done by Iran…We think it was done by Iran, because they're very inaccurate with their munitions, they have no accuracy whatsoever, it was done by Iran", Trump said on March 1.However, expert video analysis, cited by the BBC, showed that the IRGC complex next to the school was hit by a precision-guided Tomahawk missile, neither possessed by neither Iran nor Israel.Defence secretary Pete Hegseth said that US forces "never target civilian targets" and were investigating the tragedy. He later announced a higher-level investigation, led by an officer from outside US Central Command (Centcom), BBC reported.Centcom is responsible for carrying out military strikes and operations targeting Iranian assets and infrastructure.However, the US is yet to release findings of the investigation into the bombing.In May, Centcom head told a congressional committee that the investigation was "complex" as the school was "on an active IRGC cruise missile base", a claim rejected by Iran's foreign ministry as a "baseless fabrication".According to several US media reports that cited people familiar with the US military investigation, the preliminary findings concluded that it was likely outdated data supplied by the US Defence Intelligence Agency that led to the school being treated as part of a military site.Historical satellite images reportedly show the school area was previously part of the IRGC complex, but has been walled off since 2016 and has its own entrances and yards.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in parliament after far-right election win
articles.summary: Germany's chancellor clashes with AfD leader Alice Weidel, saying her migration policy amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.

Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.

Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.

It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.

The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".

The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.

Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".

While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it made a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.

Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."

Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.

As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.

Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.

"You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.

The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.

Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall ( Brandmauer ), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.

AEW and the rest of the pro wrestling world have been in full support of Brooks since she announced her diagnosis back in May. COMPLETE PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE ON OUTKICK AEW and Ring of Honor (ROH) owner Tony Khan spoke about the show in August after ROH’s Death Before Dishonor in Philadelphia. Even though she’s not on TV every week, you can believe everyone’s got Rebel in their hearts and we’ll be thinking about Rebel every week." Brooks announced her diagnosis on May 1. "The doctors have diagnosed me with terminal ALS," she said in a video. "There is not a lot of research behind ALS, and we don’t know how long I have. But it explains why I have trouble walking and talking, and all my functions will soon decline. "But now we can prepare for the future and what is to come. And I want to say thank you." Brooks joined AEW in 2019, initially as a backstage and stylist role before appearing on-screen in 2020 with Britt Baker as her personal makeup artists. She had a few matches before suffering an injury. articles.title: From intelligence sharing to missile defense, how Israel's partnership protects American security
articles.summary: Joint strikes on Iran, intelligence sharing and missile defense reveal why vilifying Israel in 2026 could prove self-defeating for the U.S.
articles.body: The anti-Israel sentiment that has been gathering momentum in the U.S. since Oct. 7, 2023, is nationally self-sabotaging. Americans should understand the ties between the U.S. and Israel are mutually beneficial and a significant portion of America’s security can be linked directly to this vital relationship. After Oct. 7, 2023, when the terrorist organization Hamas invaded Israel from Gaza and slaughtered over 1,200 victims and kidnapped another 251, the streets and campuses of America exploded with protests against the victim – Israel – while endorsing the murderous terrorist organization – Hamas. This century has never seen such a widespread response that was sympathetic to terrorists and not to victims. Fast-forward to over six months ago when the U.S. and Israel conducted joint strikes on Iranian military targets with the goal of stopping the Iranian regime from having a nuclear weapon. With on-again, off-again ceasefires and deals that have not yet resulted in a lasting peace or a change in status regarding Iran’s pursuit of nuclear weapons, some Americans are now accusing Israel of pressuring the U.S. to serve Israel’s interests, blaming the Jewish state for dragging the U.S. into an extended overseas war, using American resources to defend Israel and putting U.S. troops in harm’s way, to name only a few. ‘NO JEWS, NO NEWS’ STRIKES AGAIN AS SELECTIVE COVERAGE OF THE 'UNSETTLERS' FUELS ANTI-ISRAEL ANGER Vilifying Israel is becoming normalized in 2026 by both American politicians and voters. Some Democratic political candidates and representatives are associating themselves with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Being anti-Israel is a DSA core value; in fact, Gaza has become a central issue for the organization. In 2025, the DSA adopted a resolution making a member’s support for Israel’s right to defend itself an expellable offense. In the same year, opposition to the idea of Jews having a homeland in the historic land of Israel (Zionism) was adopted as an organizational principle. American left-wing politicians are not just paying lip-service to the DSA, they are aligning themselves with this organization that supports sanctioning America’s strongest ally in the Middle East while opposing American sanctions of oppressive and tyrannical governments such as those found in Cuba, North Korea, Iran and Venezuela. And what of the general U.S. population? An April 2026 Pew Research Center poll found "60% of U.S. adults have an unfavorable view of Israel." SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Is antisemitism behind this anti-Israel phenomenon? Absolutely – it plays a central role for the anti-Israel fanatics. But most Americans are not fanatics and in a world of social media lies, many are simply unsure of the truth, a logical byproduct of what they consume on legacy news media and social media. After the United Nations General Assembly voted to create a Jewish state in late 1947 and Israel’s subsequent proclamation of independence in May 1948, America supported Israel by being the first country to recognize the fledgling nation. The American-Israeli relationship grew over the following decades, and Israel, the only democracy in the Middle East, was seen as a vital strategic asset to America in the face of Soviet influence in the region. In a May 1968 article in the LA Times, American social philosopher Eric Hoffer wrote, "…at this moment, Israel is our only reliable and unconditional ally. We can rely more on Israel than Israel can rely on us." In the 1990s, the two countries developed a deep strategic cooperation and intelligence sharing relationship that continues today. According to the Federal Newswire, although Israel is America’s largest recipient of foreign aid, the return on investment far exceeds the cost. For example, in 2016, the U.S. agreed to provide Israel $3.8 billion per year for 10 years. Analysis shows the U.S. receives, in return, approximately $48 billion in annual benefits from this agreement. Benefits to the U.S. include Israel testing U.S. weapons systems in combat, providing intelligence to the U.S. (covering threats from Iran, its terror proxies, and the weapons each can employ against Americans), and aiding in the development of defensive missile systems – many of which have been used in the current conflict with Iran to protect American bases and allies overseas. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The FBI opened an overseas post in Tel Aviv in the mid-1990s and the FBI has had a presence there ever since. From 2020 to 2024, I was assigned to Israel as an FBI supervisory special agent focusing on counterterrorism matters with our Israeli security partners. I personally experienced the two-way exchange of intelligence with Israeli police, Shin Bet and other security services on all matters related to threats faced by both countries. I was in Israel for the horrific global event of Oct. 7 and worked around the clock with U.S. and Israeli counterparts to gather intelligence on the missing victims (including Americans), seek justice against the Hamas perpetrators and provide comfort and answers to the victims’ families. The cooperation between the two nations could not be stronger. I have previously written about how Israel is the "canary in the coal mine" when it comes to terrorism – "Israel’s experience with terrorism is often a preview of what the West can expect to see within its borders." America is safer because of Israel and – because of my official FBI tour in Israel – I can testify to this truth. The relationship between Israel and the U.S. is not based solely on shared values, history, or political support – it is also built on a deep mutual security interest that provides tangible benefits to the American people. Should Israel perish, the Holocaust will be upon us all." Americans need to realize the true quid pro quo of the U.S.-Israeli alliance before concluding Israel is a bad actor. articles.title: Bristol Airport passengers describe 'nightmare' as hundreds left stranded
articles.summary: Passengers to and from Bristol Airport say trips are "ruined", with some left to sleep in a terminal.
articles.body:
Passengers from the west of England say their holidays have been "ruined" after a UK-wide air traffic control issue caused flight cancellations and delays.

Angela Bolitho, 62, of Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, described a trip to Edinburgh with her son as a "nightmare" after their return flight to Bristol from Scotland was cancelled.

Another passenger, Liam Graham, 27, from Bradley Stoke, South Gloucestershire, said he spent seven hours sitting on a plane at Bristol Airport bound for Bodrum in Turkey before being told it could not depart.

A Bristol Airport spokesperson said flights were "mostly back to normal with a small number of delays and cancellations".

Tens of thousands of passengers were affected by the disruption on Tuesday, with a further 153 flights cancelled on Wednesday.

National Air Traffic Services (Nats) blamed a technical fault and chief executive Martin Rolfe apologised . He said there would be a full investigation after the organisation admitted fixing the problem had taken "longer than hoped".

Graham said he and his girlfriend, who were due to go on their first holiday together, boarded their easyJet flight at 13:15 BST on Tuesday and were initially told there would be a 45-minute delay.

"Two hours later, the pilot spoke to everyone individually," he said.

"He said he hadn't seen anything like it in the last 20 years and that it was unprecedented, he said to sit and see what happens."

Graham said passengers were eventually asked to leave the aircraft after seven hours.

"The pilot was devastated and working really hard to get us off the ground," he said.

"There was a swarm of 186 people trying to speak to one EasyJet guy."

EasyJet said the situation was out of its control but apologised to passengers on the flight from Bristol to Bodrum.

A spokesperson said: "We did all we can to minimise the impact on our customers, providing those on cancelled flights with options to rebook or receive a refund, securing hotel accommodation where possible, and advising those who make their own travel and accommodation arrangements on how they can be reimbursed."

Bolitho said she and her son had arrived at Edinburgh Airport on Tuesday to discover their flight home had been cancelled.

"Every hotel room in Edinburgh was sold out, we had to sleep in the airport with loads of other people," she said.

"We managed to get two seats in a cafe and get a couple of hours here and there."

The pair were subsequently rescheduled to fly home on Wednesday afternoon.

"We're sat here with everything crossed, I've been watching every EasyJet flight hasn't gone yet."

An EasyJet spokesperson said some customers due to board the flight from Edinburgh to Bristol had stayed in the terminal.

"We worked with the airport to help make them as comfortable as possible during these circumstances," they said.

Sebastian Krygier, from Brentry, Bristol, said a long-awaited birthday trip to Antalya in Turkey had been "ruined".

"We were waiting on the plane for five hours, after we were informed there was a problem with the Nats system," he said of his wait at Bristol Airport.

"Everything has been cancelled so I'm spending the holiday at home."

Alice Johnson, 23, from Shirehampton, Bristol, had been due to travel from Bristol to Zante, Greece, with friends.

"We got to the airport around 12 I think, we got on the plane at 14:30 BST and we were told to get off the plane at 17:45 BST."

Johnson said the group hoped to recover the cost of their flights but expected to lose money on their Airbnb booking.

Bristol Airport advised passengers to "check the latest flight information with their airline".

articles.title: This Hawaii company is making boats from volcanic rock and recycled plastic instead of traditional materials
articles.summary: US News: A Hawaii-based company is taking a unique approach to boat manufacturing by combining recycled plastic with volcanic rock-derived basalt fibre. Voltag.
articles.body: A Hawaii-based company is taking a unique approach to boat manufacturing by combining recycled plastic with volcanic rock-derived basalt fibre. Voltage Vessels, a startup based in Hawaii, has developed a material called ‘Eclipse X9’ which can be used in large-scale 3D printing and is being tested for marine applications. The material has already become part of the company's plans for printed boats, including a 6-metre hull submitted for US maritime defence evaluation. By replacing some conventional manufacturing processes with digital designs and printable composites, the company is exploring whether boats and marine structures could eventually be produced closer to where they are needed, instead of manufacturing them far away and then transporting them over long distances.Company in Hawaii making boats from volcanic rock and recycled plasticTraditional boatbuilding can require specialised molds, extensive labour and fixed manufacturing facilities. Voltage Vessels is exploring a different route, centred on 3D printing and a composite material called Eclipse X9.According to Defence Blog, the Hawaii-based company was founded and is led by Sam Young. Its Eclipse X9 material combines recycled PETG plastic with chopped basalt fibre, creating a structural composite designed specifically for marine and defence applications.Basalt is a volcanic rock, making it a particularly notable ingredient for a company based in Hawaii, where volcanic activity has shaped the islands. The company processes basalt fibre and recycled plastic into a material that can be used as feedstock for 3D printers.Instead of relying entirely on conventional boatbuilding methods, the approach allows a digital design to be transformed into a physical structure through additive manufacturing, or 3D printing.Eclipse X9 is built for large-scale printingAccording to 3D Printing Industry, Voltage Vessels has released Eclipse X9 for large-format additive manufacturing after several years of development. The material is now commercially available as both pellets and filament and is being evaluated at several facilities using different printing platforms.The company is targeting a wide range of uses, including marine structures, buoys, unmanned surface vehicles, infrastructure components and other structures exposed to difficult coastal conditions.Eclipse X9 is designed to work across different types of equipment rather than being tied to one specific printer. The pellet version can be used in large industrial systems, while the filament is available for machines ranging from smaller desktop printers to larger printing units.This flexibility is important to the company’s wider manufacturing idea. Instead of building every marine structure at one central factory, the material could potentially support production at facilities closer to where a finished product is required.What makes the material suitable for use in the oceanA boat material must be able to cope with long-term exposure to water, particularly saltwater. This is one of the main areas where Eclipse X9 has undergone testing. According to 3D Printing Industry, independent validation was carried out by the Advanced Structures and Composites Center at the University of Maine. The testing included mechanical assessments and analysis of the material for marine applications.In saltwater immersion trials lasting between 24-26 months, the composite retained more than 90% of its strength. The published performance figures also included tensile strength of 108.2 megapascals, bending strength of 112.98 megapascals and water absorption below 0.4 per cent.Its ability to retain strength while absorbing relatively little water is particularly important because prolonged water exposure can weaken materials used in boat hulls and other marine structures.The basalt fibre also adds properties that could make the composite suitable for specialised applications. 3D Printing Industry noted that basalt fibre is non-conductive and transparent to radio frequencies.A six-metre printed boat hull has already entered evaluationThe company’s technology is not limited to material testing. According to Defence Blog, the company has submitted a 6-metre rigid-hull inflatable boat (RHIB) for US maritime defence evaluation.RHIBs are fast boats which are commonly used for a variety of maritime operations. Traditionally, such boats can be made using materials including fibreglass or aluminium and often require specialised production facilities and tooling.The hull submitted by Voltage Vessels was printed using a large-format additive manufacturing system. The wider aim is to explore whether printed marine structures could support autonomous naval programmes and other maritime requirements.The company's broader proposal focuses on distributed manufacturing. Instead of producing boats only at a distant central facility and then shipping them to their final destination, digital designs could potentially be sent to regional manufacturing sites.The idea is to move production closer to where boats are neededDefence Blog reported that the company is thinking of Hawaii serving as an initial node in a framework intended to expand across the Indo-Pacific.Under this concept, regional facilities could use the same digital design files to produce hulls and other structural components. The process would reduce dependence on conventional molds and some of the supply chains involved in traditional boat manufacturing.This could be especially relevant in regions where transporting replacement vessels over long distances is difficult. Sending replacement hulls from the continental United States to locations across the Indo-Pacific can take considerable time and depend on available cargo transport.The company's concept is that locally available printing equipment and material could shorten that process by allowing structures to be manufactured nearer to their point of use.Recycling is another part of the company's planThe use of recycled PETG is central to Eclipse X9. According to 3D Printing Industry, the composite supports closed-loop mechanical recycling, meaning finished parts can potentially be shredded, converted back into pellets and printed again.This approach could reduce the need to simply discard used printed structures. It could also have practical value in locations where waste disposal and the delivery of new materials are both challenging.The company sees possible applications beyond boats, including ocean-monitoring equipment, coastal structures, tooling and marine infrastructure. By combining basalt fibre with recycled PETG and using large-scale 3D printing, the Hawaii company is testing whether boats of the future could be manufactured with different materials, recycled after use and produced much closer to where they are needed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Miliband rejects chief rabbi's claim British Jews in greater danger after sanctions move
articles.summary: The foreign secretary disagrees with the UK's chief rabbi who warns sanctions on Israeli settlements could put British Jews at greater risk.
articles.body:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has rejected the chief rabbi's warning that British Jews are at greater risk after the UK announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband said that as a "proud British Jew" he disagreed with UK Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis who described the move as a "truly dark day" that would "succeed only in bolstering the very extremism they seek to target".

"We all need to do more to tackle antisemitism," Miliband said, "But I believe we can do that and stand up for British values."

The sanctions on trade with illegal settlements in the West Bank come against a backdrop of rising antisemitic incidents across the UK.

The Community Security Trust (CST), an organisation that provides security support to the Jewish community, recorded 1,926 incidents of anti-Jewish hate across the UK in the first six months of 2026, a 21% increase on the same period in 2025.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham defended his government's decision, telling MPs that "Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice. Where people are being bullied out of their homes... we will always stand with the underdog."

The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".

But there has been mixed reaction within the UK Jewish community on the sanctions and possible implications for security.

The chief rabbi called the government's announcement "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric".

Sir Ephraim said: "Gesture politics of this kind feeds into an increasingly hostile discourse about Israel, and the cumulative effect of such punitive policies is to further embolden those, at home and abroad, who use hatred as a weapon against Jews."

Questioned on Mirvis's comments, Miliband said: "I don't agree with the chief rabbi, someone whom I have great respect."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme he said "anyone who holds British Jews - or indeed Jews around the world - responsible for the actions of the Israeli government, is engaging in antisemitism, pure and simple."

While, the Jewish Leadership Council (JLC) warned the sanctions move "risks becoming a de facto boycott of Israel" and accused Miliband of "yielding to pressure from the most extreme elements of British society".

And the Board of Deputies of British Jews said the decision to make the announcement before Rosh Hashanah - the Jewish New Year festival - brings "concerns for communal security at their highest levels... felt particularly acutely by British Jews".

It added the deteriorating relationship between the UK and Israel has the potential to "further inflame community tensions here too", while also noting it had warned the Israeli government over the "intolerable settler violence" that harms Israel's reputation.

Chris Mason: Burnham looks to show he will go further than Starmer with West Bank sanctions

But Na'amod - which describes itself as a movement of UK Jews seeking to end Israel's occupation and to support the equality of Palestinians and Israelis - welcomed the decision saying it had waited years for the British government to take action.

"There is no singular Jewish approach to Israel. We reject the contention that [Tuesday's] UK government measures will contribute to antisemitism."

The Movement for Progressive Judaism said "while the vulnerability of British Jews must not be ignored" measures directed at Israeli settlements "are not the same as an attack on Jews".

"We should take care not to collapse the distinction between them," it said in a statement.

The sanctions have caused a diplomatic row with Israel which has closed the British consulate in East Jerusalem and banned 11 MPs and a campaigner from the country.

On Wednesday the Israel's Diaspora Minister Amichai Chikli wrote to the head of Israeli border control recommending that several other British linked organisations and individuals should be refused entry to Israel.

The list includes Oxfam, Save the Children, Norwegian Refugee Council, Islamic Relief Worldwide, Medical Aid for Palestinians.

Speaking in the Commons on Tuesday, Miliband said the "new approach" was needed because of the plans for the E1 development - a controversial settlement project that would effectively cut off the occupied West Bank from East Jerusalem and divide the territory in two.

He also told MPs that the UK agreed there was ethnic cleansing in areas of the West Bank - accusing "settler terrorists" of driving Palestinians from their land.

"And all too often, the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this," Miliband said.

The sanctions will target companies and people providing services like construction and financing of settlements. There will also be a ban on the advertising illegal settlements in the UK. Miliband said the measures could take up to nine months to put in place.

Canada and France have also banned goods from the settles as part of a co-ordinated action with allies.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Delhi has tightened security across the national capital ahead of the 18th Brics Summit, with nearly 4,800 traffic police personnel set to manage VVIP movement and more than 35 major roads identified for traffic restrictions and diversions.The summit will be held at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi from September 11 to 13, with foreign leaders and other dignitaries expected to attend.According to ANI, Delhi Police and other security agencies have entered the final phase of preparations, with thousands of personnel deployed and heightened surveillance along routes designated for VVIP movement.Around 22 diversion points will be used to regulate traffic during the movement of foreign delegations and VVIP convoys. The main leaders' summit will be held at Bharat Mandapam on September 12 and 13, while the BRICS Business Forum is scheduled for September 11.India's Brics chairship is being guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”. The summit is expected to focus on strengthening cooperation among member and partner countries, as well as global and regional issues.India has held more than 350 BRICS meetings and high-level engagements across over 25 cities during its 2026 chairship.The 2026 summit also marks 20 years of BRICS. articles.title: Channel 4 to cut 340 jobs by the end of the year in major shake-up
articles.summary: It comes after the network conducted a review amid a "rapidly changing media landscape".
articles.body:
Channel 4 has said it plans to cut 340 jobs before the end of the year, reducing its workforce by more than a quarter.

The network, which broadcasts Gogglebox and The Great British Bake Off, will lose around 28% of its current 1,270 staff following a strategic review of the organisation.

Priya Dogra, Channel 4's chief executive, said the announcement "marks the first phase of our transformation, ensuring Channel 4 is the right shape and size to deliver its future strategy and focus investment in the programmes audiences love".

Caroline Dinenage, chair of the culture, media and sport committee said the news would be "deeply worrying for the talented and dedicated people who work at Channel 4".

The network said it planned to focus on creating a simpler and more efficient operating model and enable greater investment in distinctive programming.

In her statement, Dogra said: "Channel 4 is a precious asset which plays a unique role in the UK.

"We need to secure and own our future so we can continue to make shows others won't, reach audiences others can't, and thrive as a distinctive and disruptive British voice for future generations.

"The challenges we face require a fundamental transformation in how we work. I know the proposals we are announcing today will be very difficult for many colleagues and will have a significant impact across the organisation."

She added: "These decisions have not been taken lightly, but I strongly believe they are necessary to create a simpler, more focused and more sustainable Channel 4."

Channel 4 has faced a challenging few years as it competes with digital platforms and the shrinking advertising market for traditional TV networks.

The company referenced the rapidly changing media landscape in its press release announcing the changes, which it said includes "evolving audience habits, increasing global competition, a challenging consumer environment and a volatile advertising market".

One of Channel 4's biggest hits, Married at First Sight, is also currently off air after a BBC investigation uncovered allegations of rape and other serious misconduct.

Launched in 1982, Channel 4 is publicly owned but funded by advertising. The newly announced job cuts represent the biggest round of layoffs in the network's history.

According to Deadline, Dogra told employees on Wednesday that the redundancies will ensure that more of Channel 4's £1bn income is spent on screen.

A consultation process with staff will begin shortly, and Channel 4 said its "future strategic direction is well advanced and will be shared in the coming months".

In her statement, Dinenage said: "There are questions about what the announcement means for the broadcaster's presence in the regions, one of its success stories of recent years.

"Channel 4 is a unique asset and must find ways to maintain independence and distinctiveness while capitalising on efficiencies and opportunities for collaboration."

articles.title: Satellite images show major construction surge at Iran’s underground Pickaxe site amid US war
articles.summary: Middle East News: A suspected Iranian nuclear site buried beneath a granite mountain has seen a sharp increase in construction activity this year as the war between the.
articles.body: A suspected Iranian nuclear site buried beneath a granite mountain has seen a sharp increase in construction activity this year as the war between the US and Iran has unfolded, according to a satellite imagery analysis reviewed by CNN.The Pickaxe Mountain site, located near Iran's Natanz nuclear complex about 140 miles south of Tehran, has been the subject of sustained attention from intelligence agencies, which view it as a likely location for protecting future Iranian nuclear programme activities.A new analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), shared exclusively with CNN ahead of its publication, found “a clear surge in construction activity” at the site in 2026 after reviewing six years of satellite imagery.The CSIS analysts said the underground facility was “likely” designed as a safe haven for Iran's nuclear programme.Construction activity intensifies at underground siteAccording to the CSIS analysis, construction at Pickaxe Mountain has shifted from active excavation towards what is probably internal construction and continued reinforcement of the site's exterior.The site has seen “more road activity” in 2026 than ever before, the analysts said.The work has included raising and hardening tunnel portal accesses, paving the internal road network, reinforcing areas around the accesses and flattening and removing dirt excavated during tunnel construction.However, the CSIS analysts cautioned that the “continuous construction” observed at the site, among other factors, suggested it was “not yet capable of enrichment work, if that is the intended purpose”.The facility is “likely” designed for one of three purposes linked to Iran's nuclear programme, according to the analysis. It could serve as a centrifuge assembly facility, an enrichment facility or a safe haven for other “nuclear weapons-relevant” activities such as uranium metal conversion.Israeli intelligence has suggested that Iran may be seeking to move centrifuges to Pickaxe Mountain as part of uranium enrichment efforts.Trump threatens strike on Pickaxe MountainUS President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to strike the heavily fortified site.“We may hit Pickaxe very soon,” Trump told reporters last week, adding that “we know everybody that’s moving” at the site.Trump had also said the US could “hit” Pickaxe Mountain if it detected activity there.The US military maintains operational plans for strikes against Pickaxe Mountain, according to a source familiar with the matter cited by CNN. The site was part of a target package considered earlier this summer when Trump was threatening to escalate the conflict with Iran.The strike plan involved some of the largest bombs in the US arsenal, the source said, although it remained unclear whether those weapons could penetrate deeply enough underground to destroy whatever Iran may have moved there.The granite mountain presents a difficult target even for the Pentagon's “heaviest non-nuclear” bombs, according to the CSIS team.US works on ways to hit deeply buried sitesThe US has also been working on ways to target deeply buried underground facilities.Four days before the US launched Operation Epic Fury, a programme manager at the Defence Threat Reduction Agency signed an emergency $1.2 million contract justification to repair a “unique subterranean test facility at White Sands Missile Range” in New Mexico.The contract was for a “live-fire test designed to validate classified capabilities against rapidly emerging threats”. The document was uploaded to a federal database on February 27, the day before the war began.The memo said the “rapid test prep” needed to be completed within two to three weeks because of a “time-sensitive national security directive”.Three sources familiar with the matter told CNN that the plans were connected to the Iran war and involved developing a way to target Iran's deepest-buried underground facilities, likely including simulations of US strikes against specific nuclear sites.Satellite imagery showed excavation work beginning between February 16 and February 18 at a remote DTRA and US Strategic Command-operated site at White Sands. The location is intended to test the effects of weapons on deeply buried targets.Work continued into mid-March, when the activity appeared to halt.It could not be independently verified whether the test took place or confirm the purpose of the work observed at the DTRA site.New penetrator weapon also under developmentThe US had previously struck Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025 during Operation Midnight Hammer.Those strikes destroyed some key locations linked to Iran's nuclear programme. However, a senior US general told lawmakers last year that the deeply buried Isfahan nuclear site had only its entrances buried because the Pentagon believed its Massive Ordnance Penetrator, or MOP, bunker-busting bombs could not destroy the facility.The US military is now working on a “next generation penetrator” bomb intended to succeed the current MOP and potentially reach targets buried even deeper underground.A contract to begin developing a prototype was awarded in September 2025, while the Air Force sought defence industry sources for the new weapon in June.Pickaxe comes under renewed scrutiny amid wider warThe developments around Pickaxe Mountain come as fighting between the US and Iran has intensified again after a month of relative calm.Iran said on Wednesday that it had attacked 10 ships near the Strait of Hormuz after the US sank five Iranian oil tankers in the biggest declared wave of tit-for-tat shipping attacks since the six-month-old war began.The escalation sent Brent crude above $100 a barrel for the first time since July, while the average US retail price of diesel rose above $5.94 a gallon.Iran also said it had fired ballistic missiles at a base used by US forces in Jordan. The US and Iran have exchanged attacks on military, shipping and energy assets since the end of August.The wider conflict has also seen renewed fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen, adding another threat to energy supplies from the Middle East.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Indian family deported from Canada after asylum claim fails: 'When Canada needed Harish, he was essential'
articles.summary: Rest of World News: An Indian family that spent eight years building a life in Quebec has returned to India after Canadian authorities rejected its refugee claim and thei.
articles.body: An Indian family that spent eight years building a life in Quebec has returned to India after Canadian authorities rejected its refugee claim and their attempt to remain in the country on humanitarian grounds.The Kumar family -- Harish Kumar, his wife Sonika, and their two childrenm Goulash and Japesh -- arrived in Canada in April 2018 and sought asylum after Harish Kumar said he had left India because he believed his life was at risk. After years of legal proceedings, the family was ordered to leave Canada and boarded a flight to India on September 7.For Kumar’s two sons, the removal has meant leaving behind the only home they remember.“I grew up here,” 14-year-old Japesh Kumar told CTV News before the family’s departure. “I have friends here ... in India, I have nothing.”His 12-year-old brother, Gouresh, also spent most of his childhood in Quebec and now faces the prospect of starting over in a country he barely knows.The family was informed on August 4 that its refugee claim had been refused and that it would have to leave Canada by September 7. Kumar said his wife was detained by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) the previous week.Immigrant Workers Center, an organization that fights for the rights of immigrants, condemned the deportation and said Harish worked as a truck driver and continued transporting goods during the Covid pandemic. "When the Canadian economy needed their labor, they were called “essential workers.” Once the crisis ended, however, years of work, taxes, and contributions to their community did not protect them from deportation. This is the cruelty at the heart of the immigration system: it benefits from migrant labor while treating migrants’ lives as temporary and disposable," the organization said.Mostafa Henaway of the Immigrant Workers Centre said removing the children from Quebec after years of schooling and growing up in the province would have a significant impact on them. “I don’t think it sends a very strong signal about our values being very different than our neighbours down south in this current climate,” said Henaway.Why was the family removed?Canadian immigration authorities said removal decisions are not taken lightly and that people are removed only after legal avenues capable of stopping or delaying removal have been exhausted.The CBSA said individuals facing removal may, depending on their circumstances, have access to appeals before the Immigration and Refugee Board, judicial review applications before the Federal Court and pre-removal risk assessments.Under Section 48 of Canada's Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, once a removal order becomes enforceable, CBSA is required to remove the individual “as soon as possible”.For the Kumar family, the process stretched across eight years before ending with their return to India.What happened in India?When Harish came to Canada, he said he had to flee India after he was arrested and mistreated by police after he "refused to give money to people associated with political groups." According to a Change.org petition that was started before the family's deportation, Harish owned a small grocery store in Goraya City, Punjab. He was approached for money for an election campaign."Two men arrived at his store on a motorcycle, apparently presenting themselves as customers purchasing supplies for a wedding. After leaving the store, they positioned their motorcycle across from the shop. He says that police officers subsequently arrived with individuals he believed were connected to political groups and accused him of illegally parking the motorcycle...police claimed to have found questionable materials on the motorcycle and arrested him. From August 12 to August 16, 2017, he (Harish) reports that he was held in custody, with his hands bound behind his back, and repeatedly kicked, pulled to the ground, and beaten with a stick," the campaign statement read.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1927, Paramount bought a 2,700-acre California ranch and filmed more than 160 movies there; after wildfire destroyed almost everything in 2018, a $26 million rebuild is nearly complete
articles.summary: US News: For nearly a century, Paramount Ranch in California's Santa Monica Mountains was linked to Hollywood filmmaking. The 2,700-acre property was bought by.
articles.body: For nearly a century, Paramount Ranch in California's Santa Monica Mountains was linked to Hollywood filmmaking. The 2,700-acre property was bought by Paramount Pictures in 1927 and used as an outdoor filming location. Between 1927 and 1943, the studio made more than 130 films at the ranch.The ranch was used for productions set in different parts of the world. Over the years, it became known for its Western-style sets and was also used for television productions. Stars including Gary Cooper, Bob Hope and the Marx Brothers filmed there. TV shows such as Gunsmoke, The Dukes of Hazzard and The Bachelor also used the ranch as a filming location.The Park Service acquired Paramount Ranch in 1980, two years after the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area was established by Congress. The site is described by NPS as the only location in the National Park System dedicated to telling the story of American filmmaking, both past and present.The ranch was also open to the public, with visitors able to hike, bike and ride horses on its trails. It hosted events including ranger programmes, music festivals, classic movie nights, weddings and night sky parties.Woolsey Fire destroyed historic ranchThe Woolsey Fire began on November 8, 2018, and burned nearly 100,000 acres across Ventura and Los Angeles counties. The fire reached Paramount Ranch on November 9 and destroyed most of its historic buildings and film sets."Almost everything in the ranch burned," said Jody Lyle, Superintendent of the Santa Monica Mountains National Recreation Area.Lyle said a few structures survived, including some film sets, the chapel from HBO's Westworld and the train depot from Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman. However, most of what visitors knew as Western Town was destroyed.The loss was significant because the ranch had continued its connection with filmmaking for decades. According to Lyle, Paramount Pictures had owned the property from 1927 to 1943 and filmed more than 160 movies there during that period. The property was later developed with a Western Town-style setting, where television Westerns and other productions were filmed.Although Western Town was the most recognisable part of the site, Lyle said the older buildings behind the facades were particularly important to the ranch's history. Many of the Western Town sets had been built in the 1980s and 1990s, while the original buildings dated back to the late 1920s and early 1930s.Rebuilding follows historic footprintsAlmost eight years after the fire, a $26 million rebuilding project is nearing completion. The aim is to restore Paramount Ranch as a place for filmmaking while also creating space for public events, education and other activities.The new buildings are being constructed in the footprints of structures that existed during the historic Paramount era. The National Park Service says the first phase includes four structures: a Pavilion, Prop Shed, Barn and restrooms. The buildings are designed to be fire-safe and adaptable."What we have rebuilt here is something more akin to what existed during the Paramount era," Lyle said.The Pavilion is a covered event space that can accommodate more than 200 people. The NPS lists its planned capacity as 265 people. The Barn will provide indoor event space for 200 people, while the Prop Shed will accommodate 100 people. New restrooms will also support large events and day-use visitors.The rebuilt site includes underground utilities and modern facilities. The new structures have been designed with wildfires in mind, with metal roofs, fire-resistant siding and built-in fire sprinkler systems.Movie sets to returnOnce the new buildings are complete, the National Park Service plans to work with film companies, partner organisations and volunteers to bring movie sets back to Paramount Ranch.The new infrastructure will allow studios to build facades suited to individual film and television productions. Some sets will be temporary and will only be accessible while filming is taking place. Others will be designed to remain for longer periods and could be used for educational purposes."This is going to be an amazing facility for us. Having this area where more than 200 people can gather for all kinds of different events will be great," Lyle said.The rebuilding effort received $26 million in federal disaster relief funding. The Santa Monica Mountains Fund, a non-profit organisation, also raised $1 million to help start the reconstruction project.The National Park Service and the fund have said they are committed to bringing back the ranch's filmmaking tradition while also creating opportunities for people to gather, take part in education programmes and volunteer in habitat restoration.The ranch's buildings remain closed to the public while construction continues. However, its trails remain open for hiking, biking and horseback riding.The National Park Service expects the rebuilt Paramount Ranch to reopen in 2027, marking the ranch's centennial year.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Reigning Miss Austria beauty queen Lucia Sisic dies aged 22
articles.summary: Tributes have been paid to Lucia Sisic, who had a lifelong experience with a heart condition.
articles.body:
Reigning Miss Austria beauty queen Lucia Sisic has died at the age of 22, having experienced a lifelong heart condition.

Mission Austria, which runs the Miss Austria and Mister Austria beauty pageants, announced the news in a tribute on its Facebook page on Monday, saying: "It is with great shock and deep sorrow that we have learned of the passing of our Miss Austria 2024, Lucia Sisic."

No cause of death has yet been confirmed.

Sisic was crowned Miss Austria in 2024 and remained the reigning titleholder as no subsequent contest has yet been staged.

In its Facebook post, translated from German, Mission Austria said: "We will remember Lucia as a wonderful young woman.

"Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences go out to her family, friends, and all those close to her during this difficult time."

The message, signed by Mission Austria CEO Kerstin Rigger and her husband Jörg, added Sisic "will always remain a part of our Miss Austria family".

As a public figure, Sisic had spoken openly about her health condition. In 2024, she shared a post on Instagram thanking her paediatric medical team who looked after her as a young person.

"Thanks to the medical staff and the dedicated doctors - who time and again saved my life through their tremendous efforts - I have overcome many difficult moments and been able to lead a fulfilling life," she wrote at the time.

Speaking to Austrian outlet Heute in 2024, the Miss Austria winner said her first operation was right after her birth.

She also spoke of how her health impacted her childhood.

"Sports weeks took place without me. My childhood was simply different, but it also made me strong," she said.

Herzkinder Österreich, a charity in Austria which supports children with heart conditions, also paid tribute to Sisic.

In a Facebook post, the organisation said it is "deeply saddened by the untimely death" of Sisic, adding "at just 22 years old, she left us far too soon".

The tribute says: "Lucia herself was a true child at heart. A young woman who knew what it meant to grow up with a congenital heart defect, to endure surgeries, and still to pursue her own path with courage and joy.

"We will remember her as a warm-hearted, joyful, and impressive young woman – and as an adult child who wanted to give courage to others affected."
